newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals - Japan molybdenum still as prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals - Japan molybdenum still as prices fall.

text.p: Molybdenum trade was at a standstill in Japan as prices retraced from their recent surge, with well-stocked consumers shunning the market and a large gap separating bids and offers, traders said on Tuesday.
"We're at a standoff," said one molybdenum trader at a large trade house. "Users have stocks, and people are waiting to see what happens."
He noted that while molybdenum oxide prices were above $5.50 a lb just a few weeks ago, now offers at $4.50 were finding no buyers and bids were down at $3.60 to $3.70.

He blamed the pullback on a drop-off in European demand as a recent spate of buying appeared to have run its course, and expected the market to remain deadlocked until fresh demand emerged for the first quarter of next year.
The weakness was also reflected in ferro-molybdenum prices, with offers for Chinese metal noted below $12 a kg, he said.

Molybdenum prices had risen sharply this year, fueled in part by a drop in projected output from Chilean state-owned copper producer Codelco to 30 million lbs this year from 37 million lbs in 1995 as ore grades deteriorated.
Also fueling the rise was a drop in exports from China.

Song Xiaoying, managing director of Shangxiang Minmetals Ltd, told Reuters in Hong Kong that Chinese molybdenum exports this year up to the end of July were 12.74 million lbs, well below the rate of the past two years. Exports totalled 31.53 million lbs for all of 1995 and 37.31 million lbs for 1994.
He added that while China's average annual output, at 38 million lbs, and exports have remained relatively stable, long-term mining at major deposits in north China had depleted reserves.
"We have no material to sell on a spot basis," he said. Shangxiang Minmetals is one of the biggest traders of Chinese non-ferrous and strategic metals.
A Japanese trader countered, however, that exports from China, unlike those of Chile, fell due to growing domestic demand rather than a drop in supply. "They have the goods," he said.
He predicted molybdenum oxide prices would eventually stabilise between $4.00 and $5.00 per lb.

In the ferroalloy market, Japanese traders said most of Japan's large ferrochrome users had agreed, as expected, to keep charge chrome prices at 42 cents per lb on a cost, insurance and freight basis in the fourth quarter, unchanged from the previous quarter.
--Edmund Klamann, Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-6179, Lynne O'Donnell, Hong Kong News Desk +85-2-2843-6470
